lessons.title: Planning intake and managing cattle flow
lessons.html:
The supervisor's role

Controlling a feedlot production unit means making sure that cattle, feed, people and facilities work together every day to produce slaughter-ready cattle at the lowest cost per kilogram, with good animal welfare and safe beef. The supervisor plans, checks, records and corrects.

Planning intake

  • Match the number of cattle bought to available pen space, feed stocks and staff.
  • Know the source: cattle from many small sellers or long transport are higher risk for respiratory disease and need more care on arrival.
  • Plan pen allocation so that cattle of similar weight and type are grouped.
  • Check that receiving pens have clean water, good hay and dry footing.

Receiving and processing

On arrival, check documents and identity, count and weigh the cattle, and record arrival weight and condition. Let them rest with water and hay. Process them according to the vet's program: identification, vaccination, internal and external parasite treatment and any implant or additive programs the feedlot uses legally. Record every product, batch number and withdrawal period.

Managing pen density and flow

Overcrowded pens cause stress, poor bunk access, mud and more disease. Follow the feedlot's standard for space per animal and bunk length per animal. Move cattle between pens only when needed, and plan marketing so that pens are emptied, cleaned and repaired before the next group arrives.

Marketing

Cattle should be sent to slaughter when they reach the target weight and fat cover for the market grade the feedlot aims at. Keeping cattle too long wastes feed because feed conversion gets worse as cattle get fatter. Check that no animal in a withdrawal period is loaded.

lessons.title: Controlling feed and nutrition
lessons.html:
Feed is the biggest cost

Feed usually makes up the largest share of feedlot costs after the purchase of the cattle. Small errors in mixing, delivery or waste add up to large losses.

Control points

  1. Ingredient receiving – weigh every load, check moisture, mould, foreign matter and smell, and reject poor loads. Keep delivery notes and supplier analyses.
  2. Storage – keep commodities dry, covered and separated, use oldest stock first, and control rodents and birds. Manage silage faces to limit spoilage.
  3. Mixing – check mixer scales regularly, compare loaded amounts with the ration sheet daily, and investigate differences.
  4. Delivery – compare delivered kilograms per pen with the call from the bunk reader.
  5. Bunk management – consistent bunk reading and feeding times.

Step-up programs

Rations are changed from high-roughage starter to high-energy finisher in steps set by the nutritionist. Skipping steps or feeding the wrong ration to a pen can cause acidosis, bloat and deaths. The supervisor checks that ration changes happen as planned and watches pens closely afterwards.

Feed additives

Some rations contain additives such as ionophores, buffers or growth promoters. These must be registered, used at the inclusion rate set by the nutritionist and according to the label under Act 36 of 1947. Some are toxic to other species such as horses, so keep feed away from them.

Stock control

Do a regular stock count of all commodities and reconcile it with purchases and usage. Unexplained differences point to waste, theft or mixing errors and must be followed up.

lessons.title: Animal health, welfare and staff
lessons.html:
Health program

Work with the feedlot vet to set the health protocol: processing products, treatment protocols for common diseases, and criteria for pulling, treating, re-treating and culling. The supervisor makes sure the protocol is followed exactly.

  • Pen riders check every pen daily, early in the morning when sick cattle are easiest to spot.
  • Pulled animals are examined, temperatures taken where required, and treated according to protocol.
  • Every treatment is recorded with the animal number, product, dose, date and withdrawal period.
  • Dead animals are recorded and, where the vet requires, examined to find the cause.
  • Medicines are stored as the label says, stock is controlled, and used needles go into sharps containers.

Welfare

The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 applies. Provide shade where possible, clean water at all times, dry pens and enough bunk space. Handle cattle with low-stress methods. Animals that cannot recover must be humanely euthanased by an authorised, trained person under the vet's direction, not left to suffer.

Managing people

A feedlot depends on routine. Give each worker clear duties and daily targets, train them in their tasks and in safety, and check the work. Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993 the employer must provide a safe workplace: machine guards, protective equipment, safe handling facilities and training. Hold a short meeting at the start of the day to plan work and share problems. Recognise good work and deal with poor performance fairly and consistently.

Emergencies

Have plans for fire, machinery breakdown, water failure, power failure and disease outbreaks, including who to call. A pen without water on a hot day is an emergency.

lessons.title: Measuring performance and controlling costs
lessons.html:
Key performance indicators

You control what you measure. A feedlot unit is judged on a few main indicators, calculated per pen and for the whole unit.

IndicatorHow it is worked out
Average daily gain (ADG)Weight gained divided by days on feed
Feed conversion ratio (FCR)Kg feed eaten divided by kg weight gained
MorbidityNumber of cattle treated divided by number in the group
MortalityNumber of deaths divided by number in the group
Cost of gainTotal feed, health and other costs divided by kg gained

Example

A pen of 100 steers arrives at 230 kg and leaves 110 days later at 450 kg. Gain is 220 kg per head, so ADG is 2.0 kg per day. If each steer ate 1 320 kg of feed, the FCR is 1 320 divided by 220, which is 6.0. If the feed cost R4.50 per kg, the feed cost of gain is R27 per kg. Compare this with the price received to judge the margin.

Using the numbers

Compare pens, suppliers, rations and seasons. A pen with poor ADG and high morbidity may point to a high-risk supplier or poor processing. A rising FCR across the unit may point to mixing errors, feed spoilage or cattle kept too long. Discuss results with the manager, the nutritionist and the vet, and agree on actions.

Records

Keep complete records: arrivals, weights, processing, feed delivered, treatments, deaths, sales and abattoir results. Good records protect the business in disputes and support traceability.

Key points

  • Plan intake to match pens, feed and staff, and process cattle according to the vet's program.
  • Control feed at every step: receiving, storage, mixing, delivery and bunk management.
  • Follow health protocols and record every treatment and withdrawal period.
  • Train and supervise staff and keep the workplace safe.
  • Track ADG, FCR, morbidity, mortality and cost of gain, and act on the results.
